beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Hunger After All the Worlds makes worldbuilding answer to its inhabitants.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This novel pairs encounters with an atlas of how speculative ideas work.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: In the story, Aster builds worlds that no longer surprise her.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Her pupils explore inventions whose consequences resist a tidy classification.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers follow a changed rule into relationships, institutions, and lived costs.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The story then asks what even that careful method might miss.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Consider the book’s example of a library containing every possible book.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The information is abundant, but choosing what matters remains difficult.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Our reader still needs one useful selection before time runs out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: More available books do not automatically make that choice easier.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The atlas calls attention to this movement of scarcity.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It asks what a new possibility changes, rather than merely naming it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: For example, copied minds can enter different branches of time.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Two people share a past, but their futures separate.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Which obligations travel with both, and which must change?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The atlas turns that unusual premise into a social question.
